---
title: "Semester project"
subtitle: "From messy data to a defensible data architecture"
---

## Purpose

The project revisits one authentic data problem throughout the semester. The goal is not to accumulate unrelated features; it is to show how database theory changes the quality of an evolving design.

::: {.design-question}
Your final claim should answer: Why is this representation and division of work appropriate for the stated users, rules, and workload?
:::

## Acceptable project domains

Strong candidates include transportation, environmental monitoring, biodiversity, housing, public health, energy, sports, astronomy, or an approved organizational dataset. A project must contain enough structure to motivate relationships and constraints, enough volume or query complexity to investigate performance, and an analytical question that benefits from Parquet/DuckDB/Polars. A spatial phase is preferred; an alternative specialization requires approval.

## Phases and evidence

| Phase | Main deliverable | Evidence expected |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Requirements | Stakeholders, questions, rules, conceptual model | Assumptions, examples, counterexamples |
| 2. Relational implementation | PostgreSQL DDL, ingestion, representative queries | Constraint tests and data-quality checks |
| 3. Correctness | Dependency, normalization, and transaction analysis | Anomalies prevented or deliberately accepted |
| 4. Performance | Workload, index hypothesis, benchmark | Plans and measurements before/after |
| 5. Analytics | Parquet representation plus DuckDB/Polars analysis | Cross-engine comparison and data-movement discussion |
| 6. Specialization and defense | Spatial or approved extension; architecture memo | Reproducibility, tradeoffs, limitations, ethical considerations |

## Final package

1. A concise architecture/design memo written for a technically literate stakeholder.
2. Reproducible schema, ingestion, queries, and analysis.
3. A data dictionary and provenance statement.
4. Tests or checks for core integrity requirements.
5. Query-plan and benchmark evidence for at least one meaningful design decision.
6. A short presentation and question period.

## Draft rubric

| Dimension | Weight |
|---|---:|
| Requirements and model fitness | 20% |
| Correctness and integrity | 20% |
| Query and analytical quality | 15% |
| Performance reasoning and evidence | 15% |
| Reproducibility and technical communication | 15% |
| Design defense, tradeoffs, ethics, and limitations | 15% |

Milestone feedback is formative: students are expected to revise earlier decisions when later evidence exposes a weakness.
